title: Container Ship
body:
Container Ship is a cargo ship built to carry standardised shipping containers stacked on deck and in holds, moved by giant cranes at specialised ports. Container ships carry most of the world's manufactured goods, and the largest now hold over twenty-four thousand containers.

Container ships made global trade cheap and fast, and their standard box reshaped ports, warehouses, and shopping.

title: Oil Tanker
body:
Oil Tanker is a ship built to carry liquid cargo, chiefly crude oil and refined products, in large tanks within its hull. Oil tankers range from coastal product tankers to very large crude carriers of over three hundred thousand tonnes.

Oil tankers are the energy system's sea transport, and their safety and spill-prevention design are matters of public regulation.

title: Bulk Carrier
body:
Bulk Carrier is a cargo ship built to carry unpackaged bulk goods — grain, coal, ore, and cement — in large holds with wide hatches. Bulk carriers are the work horses of raw-material trade, moving the ingredients of industry and food.

Bulk carriers move the raw stuff of civilisation, and their holds are the granaries and coal bunkers of the sea.

title: Ferry Ship
body:
Ferry Ship is a ship that carries passengers and vehicles on regular routes, larger and more seaworthy than a river ferry. Ferry ships serve island nations and strait crossings, with car decks, passenger lounges, and timetables that communities depend on.

Ferry ships are lifelines for island communities, and their reliability is a public service.

title: Icebreaker
body:
Icebreaker is a ship built to break through sea ice, with a reinforced hull, a rounded bow that rides up onto ice, and powerful engines. Icebreakers keep Arctic and Antarctic routes open, resupply polar stations, and rescue beset vessels.

Icebreakers are the polar work horses, and their design is a triumph of shipbuilding against nature's hardest material.

title: Sailing Ship: Cutty Sark
body:
Sailing Ship: Cutty Sark was a British tea clipper launched in 1869, built for speed on the China tea trade, and now preserved as a museum ship in Greenwich, London. Cutty Sark's sleek hull and towering rig made her one of the fastest sailing ships of her age.

Cutty Sark is a public fact of maritime history, and her preservation keeps the age of sail visible to modern visitors.
